name: Ben Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ben. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on response at the south station, down by the old docks, which is warehouses, student flats and a couple of rough pubs. About one shift in three I get put in the custody suite instead, that's the cells where we book people in, take their details and check on them every hour. I like the variety, honestly, one day a burglary in a student house and the next day a lorry driver with no paperwork. What tires me out is the form-filling in custody, the same questions forty times a night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about your life outside work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with Marco, an old school friend who works in a warehouse office, so the rent's split and it's not bad. I play five-a-side on Wednesdays when the rota lets me. My parents run a café near the bus station, and I still help out some Sundays. I've got about four months of money saved, and I'm slowly putting a bit aside for my own place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So a few things get quicker and that's it. Fair enough. That sounds believable, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, a bit of help with the boring parts and nothing more. At work I'd probably say, good, maybe the custody forms will fill themselves in now. I don't post much online, mostly football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means not a lot changes for me, and I'm fine with that. The pay's normal, the job's steady, and the rent's manageable with Marco. My only real thought is whether to stay on response long term or go for something specialist, but that's my choice, not AI's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing response and custody shifts. I'd use the AI tool on my phone now and then, like I do now, to help me revise the law for my next assessment. And I'd keep putting a hundred and fifty a month aside for a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Picturing it, it's just a normal Tuesday. The kettle in custody is still broken and someone still hasn't fixed the printer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI to revise. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll type in something like 'explain the difference between theft and robbery like I'm new', and it gives me a clear answer with examples. Then I check it against the training notes, because the AI got a point about search powers wrong once. It's handy, not something I'd trust blind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave policing, if anything, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay, probably, if the gap got too big. Marco earns about the same as me in a warehouse office with no night shifts and nobody spitting at him. But I like the job, so I'd stay unless something really changed.

say: It's **what he expected**: a bit of help with boring tasks.
Maybe the **custody forms** will finally fill themselves in.
think: His **job is steady** and rent is manageable with a flatmate.
His real question is **response or specialist**, his own choice.
Pay compared with **office jobs** is the only pull to leave.
do: Use the **AI app** now and then to revise law.
Save **a hundred and fifty** a month for a deposit.
feel: **Calm**, picturing a normal Tuesday in custody.
Mildly **amused** by the broken kettle and printer.
S0.quote: The AI got a point about search powers wrong once. It's handy, not something I'd trust blind.
fieldNote: A measured, **numbers-minded** voice; no strong views either way.
Already uses AI **occasionally** and checks it against notes.
His only pull from policing is **pay** compared with easier jobs.

steps.text: Keep working response and custody shifts at the south station
Save a hundred and fifty a month towards a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, checking, booking. That's custody, pretty much. Booking people in is the whole thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's about time, the custody forms are the worst part of the job. I'd be fine with the software if it's been tested properly and someone signs it off. I'd say that to my sergeant too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think custody changes a lot and I get pushed back onto the street more. That's fine by me, but it means fewer of those quiet custody shifts where you can catch up, and maybe less overtime, because custody overtime was easy money. I'd also be watching for the force deciding it needs fewer of us overall, though I don't think that happens quickly in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the system was in and the first few weeks of mistakes were sorted, I'd use it properly and learn the shortcuts. I'd keep saving, maybe bump it to two hundred a month in case the overtime dries up. And I'd look at the dog unit or roads policing, because they're hands-on and harder to put on a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit unsettled. Not scared, more like when they changed the shift pattern and you had to work out your whole life again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Marco? Does this picture touch him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco does stock ordering and booking deliveries in a warehouse office, so yes, a lot. I'd tell Marco to learn whatever system they bring in before they bring it in. If he lost his job, I'd cover the rent for a couple of months, but not forever, I'm not made of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does that overtime matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's maybe two hundred a month on average, which is my deposit money, basically. So if custody goes mostly digital, my flat gets pushed back a year or so. Annoying, but not the end of the world.

He'd back the software once it's **tested and signed off**.
think: Custody goes digital and he's pushed **back on the street**.
Easy **custody overtime**, his deposit money, would shrink.

do: Learn the **custody system** properly once early bugs are fixed.
Raise savings to **two hundred** a month.
Look at the **dog unit** or roads policing.
S1.quote: If custody goes mostly digital, my flat gets pushed back a year or so. Annoying, but not the end of the world.
fieldNote: He sees the **overtime loss** before the job loss, a very practical lens.
Considers **hands-on specialist** units as a hedge.
Worry for his **flatmate's** office job is real but bounded.

steps.text: Learn the new custody booking system once bugs are fixed
Raise monthly savings to two hundred to replace lost overtime
Ask about places on the dog unit or roads policing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. Two years. Right. That's a big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down and think it through: who's responsible when the machine gets it wrong in custody, and what happens to the staff. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it. I'd back the association if they pushed for a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think by 2028 a lot of police thinking work goes: custody, reports, call sorting, maybe even some investigation. The force would keep street officers because the robots aren't ready till 2031, but they'd need fewer of us in the station. After 2031, I don't know. I'd be twenty-nine, which is young enough to start again but not without savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push my savings hard, cutting the takeaways and the weekend trips, aiming for six months by 2028. I'd apply for the dog unit straight away, because handling a dog is about as hands-on as policing gets. And I'd use the AI tools every day, because if they're running the station, I want to understand them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. Not panicking, I've got some money and I'm young. But I'd feel like I was building on sand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about three years after. What would you do in those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use them. Three years of hands-on policing while I think about what's next, and build up as much money as I can. I might also learn something from my dad in the café, honestly, because people still want a person making their coffee, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'building on sand'. What's the sand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The idea that any job is safe for long. My parents built the café over twenty years. I'd be planning my life in three-year chunks, and that's not how I thought adult life would go.

He'd back the **association** if it pushed for a plan.
think: By 2028, custody, reports and **call sorting** go to AI.
The force needs **fewer in the station**, keeping street officers till 2031.
At twenty-nine he could restart, but **only with savings**.
do: Cut takeaways and trips to reach **six months** saved by 2028.
Apply to the **dog unit** straight away.
Use the AI tools **every day** to understand them.
feel: Like **building on sand**, planning in three-year chunks.
S2.quote: I'd be planning my life in three-year chunks, and that's not how I thought adult life would go.
fieldNote: Uses the **robot gap** as a window to save and stay hands-on.
His parents' **café** quietly sits in the back as a fallback.
Fast timeline moves him from occasional to **daily AI use**.

steps.text: Cut takeaways and trips to reach six months saved
Apply to the dog unit in the next intake
Use the force's AI tools daily on every shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots by 2034. Okay, that's more like a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this properly, and the force should start planning now: which jobs change, what training people get. I'd want them to be straight with us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's manageable. By 2031 I'd hope to be in the dog unit with a few years in, which is about as hands-on as you get, and safe till 2034 at least. That's eight years of steady work, which is plenty of time to save for my own place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to the dog unit next year. I'd keep saving two hundred a month and buy a small flat around 2029, before things move. And I'd learn the AI tools as they come into the force, at a normal pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a controlled way. Like knowing your contract ends in five years. You can plan around that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy a flat before things move? Some would wait.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a mortgage I can afford on one police wage is safer than renting if prices go mad. If I lose the job later I can rent a room out. My dad bought the café building when everyone said wait, and it's the reason they're comfortable now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The civilian staff in custody and the control room. They're good people, and their jobs are basically thinking work. Five years is time to retrain, but only if somebody pays for it.

say: The force should be **straight with staff** about what changes.
Planning should name **which jobs change** and what training follows.
think: By 2031 he'd hope to be in the **dog unit**, safe till 2034.
That's **eight years** of steady work to save.
Civilian staff need **paid retraining** to cope.
do: Apply to the **dog unit** next year.
Buy a **small flat** around 2029 before prices shift.
Learn AI tools at a **normal pace**.
feel: Like a **contract** ending in five years: plannable.
S3.quote: A mortgage I can afford on one police wage is safer than renting if prices go mad.
fieldNote: Five years gives him an **eight-year** horizon he finds comfortable.
Copies his father's **property instinct**: buy before others do.
Shows concern for **civilian colleagues** but stays practical.

steps.text: Apply to the dog unit next year
Buy a small flat around 2029 on one police wage
Learn each AI tool as the force brings it in

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's practically a different person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get it right, so there's no excuse for anyone being caught out. I'd tell my mates to plan, but I wouldn't make a big deal of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd have twelve years in by 2036, probably in the dog unit or roads policing, and the robots aren't until 2039. If it does go then, I'd be in my late thirties with a flat paid down a bit, which is a decent place to start again from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my plan: dog unit, flat, and maybe a sergeant's exam if I'm good enough by then. I'd keep using the AI tools now and then, more as they get better. I wouldn't change much this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years' warning is a bit like knowing the café will need a new roof. You put a bit aside and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make ten years feel shorter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the force froze hiring for promotions to save money, then I'd be stuck at constable with no way up. That's happened before. But I'd still have work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Marco in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Marco to start a course now, part-time, something with his hands or with people. Ten years is a long time to drift. He'd probably say I'm being dramatic.

say: Ten years means **no excuse** for being caught out.
He'd tell friends to **plan quietly** without making a fuss.
think: By 2036 he'd have **twelve years in**, maybe in the dog unit.
Robots around **2039** leave him a decent restart point.
A **part-paid flat** gives him a cushion.
do: Stick to the plan: **dog unit**, flat, maybe sergeant's exam.
Use AI tools **more often** as they improve.
feel: **Calm**, like planning for a roof repair years away.
S4.quote: Ten years' warning is a bit like knowing the café will need a new roof. You put a bit aside and get on with it.
fieldNote: With a decade's notice he sees **no threat** to his own work or money.
His only fear is a **promotion freeze**, an old-style risk.
Pushes his **flatmate** to act while staying relaxed himself.

steps.text: Carry on response work and apply to the dog unit
Use AI tools more on shift as they improve
Buy a small flat within the next three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be twenty-nine with three years of hands-on work left and no clear next step. What would help is the force being honest early about which posts go, and paying for training in something hands-on, while we're still earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what young officers want. People assume we joined for a job for life. Most of us joined to help people and get a decent wage. If that changes, tell us early and we'll adapt.

headlineQuote: Most of us joined to help people and get a decent wage. If that changes, tell us early and we'll adapt.
portrait: A 27-year-old **response officer** at a south side station, often covering the **custody suite**.
Shares a flat with a school friend, saves for a deposit and helps at his parents' **café**.
Pragmatic and measured; uses AI **now and then** and checks it against his notes.
Sees **lost overtime** first, then station cuts; plans a move to the hands-on **dog unit**.
Calm in slow worlds, **anxious** only when AGI lands in two years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving him three years of hands-on work and no next step.
whatWouldHelp: **Early honesty** about which posts go, and **paid training** in hands-on work.
